beats.headline: Why did Java break the classpath?
beats.subline: The flat classpath was a disaster waiting to happen. Here is how Project Jigsaw fixed it.
beats.narration: For twenty years, Java relied on a flat classpath. You dumped JARs in a folder, and the JVM searched them linearly. If two JARs had the same class, the first one won, causing silent, nightmare-inducing runtime bugs.

beats.title: Classpath vs. Module Path

bottom.label: JPMS Module Path
points: Fails fast if modules are missing

beats.narration: The old classpath was a black box. JPMS introduces a module graph. Now, the JVM verifies your entire dependency tree before executing a single line of code, ensuring no missing or duplicate modules.

beats.title: The module-info.java Descriptor

steps.explanation: Defines explicit dependencies. 'transitive' forces downstream consumers to also read the dependency.
Only classes in this package are visible to other modules. Everything else is hidden.
Grants deep reflection access to specific frameworks, keeping your internals private otherwise.

beats.narration: Your module-info file is the source of truth. It explicitly defines what you require, what you export to the public, and which internal packages you open for reflection-heavy frameworks like Hibernate.

beats.title: Module Encapsulation
beats.subtitle: Who can see what?
beats.narration: JPMS enforces strict boundaries. If a package isn't exported, it's invisible. If it isn't opened, reflection attempts will throw an InaccessibleObjectException. It's security by design.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
takeaways: Classpath is a flat, fragile list
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): Handling the 'Unnamed Module' and migration →
beats.narration: That's the foundation. In Part 2, we tackle the migration nightmare: how to handle legacy JARs that don't have a module descriptor.

beats.headline: Your legacy JARs are breaking the module system.
beats.subline: You can't just flip a switch. Here is the bridge for modularizing existing codebases.
beats.narration: You have a massive app with fifty dependencies. None of them have a module-info file. If you try to modularize, your build will crash. You need the migration bridge.

beats.title: Module Types
beats.narration: Automatic modules are your best friend. By adding an Automatic-Module-Name to your manifest, the JVM treats legacy JARs as modules, allowing your new code to require them safely.

beats.title: The Split Package Error
beats.caption: The #1 migration killer

lines.text: # Trying to use two JARs with the same package

beats.narration: JPMS forbids split packages. If two modules contain the same package, the JVM fails at startup. You must either merge the JARs or rename the packages to keep the graph valid.

beats.title: The --patch-module Escape Hatch

steps.explanation: Injects classes into an existing module. Use this for testing or patching legacy code without re-compiling.

beats.narration: Need a quick fix? Use patch-module to inject classes into a module at runtime. It's a temporary escape hatch for testing, not a long-term architectural solution.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
takeaways: Patch-module is for testing, not production
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): Slimming down the JDK with jlink →
beats.narration: You're ready to modularize. In Part 3, we use jlink to strip the JDK down to a 40MB runtime image. No more 300MB Docker containers.

beats.headline: Your Docker images are 300MB too heavy.
beats.subline: The standard JDK includes everything but the kitchen sink. Let's trim the fat.
beats.narration: A full JDK is massive because it bundles Swing, CORBA, and tools you never use. jlink lets you build a custom JRE containing only the modules your application actually needs.

beats.title: Discovering Dependencies
beats.caption: Use jdeps to find your required modules
beats.narration: Run jdeps on your JAR. It analyzes your bytecode and tells you exactly which JDK modules are required. This list is your input for the linker.

beats.title: The jlink Command

steps.explanation: Only include the modules jdeps identified.
Removes debug info, man pages, and headers to save space.
Uses zip compression to shrink the image further.

beats.narration: This command creates a tiny runtime image. By stripping debug info and compressing, you can drop your runtime size from hundreds of megabytes to under 50.

beats.title: The jlink Pipeline
beats.subtitle: From fat JDK to slim JRE
beats.narration: The pipeline is simple: analyze, filter, and link. The result is a self-contained runtime ready for production, perfectly tailored to your app's specific footprint.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
takeaways: jlink builds a minimal JRE image
Strip debug info and compress for size

beats.narration: You now have a lean, mean production image. In Part 4, we wrap up with the final boss: handling deep reflection and the unnamed module.

beats.headline: Why is your reflection code failing?
beats.subline: JPMS kills deep reflection by default. Here is how to fix it without losing security.
beats.narration: Frameworks like Jackson and Hibernate love reflection. But JPMS blocks setAccessible(true) on closed packages. If you don't configure your modules, your app will crash with an InaccessibleObjectException.

beats.title: The Reflection Error
beats.caption: The dreaded InaccessibleObjectException
beats.narration: The JVM is protecting your internals. It says the module does not open the package to the caller. You have two choices: open the package or grant access via command line flags.

beats.title: The --add-opens Escape Hatch

steps.explanation: Allows deep reflection from the unnamed module into a specific JDK package.
Grants reflection access only to the specific framework that needs it.

beats.narration: Use add-opens to grant reflective access. Prefer qualified opens to specific frameworks over ALL-UNNAMED. It keeps your security posture tight while allowing your libraries to function.

beats.title: Module Access Summary
beats.narration: Remember: exports is for your API, opens is for your frameworks. Don't mix them up. Keeping them separate is how you maintain a clean, secure, and modular architecture.

beats.title: Chapter Complete
beats.narration: You've mastered JPMS. Check out the roadmap link for the full lab and verified code samples. Time to modularize your production services.
